name: print a rule that gives a start without thinking
one_line: A mechanical procedure printed beside a hard task, runnable by anybody without deciding anything, which leaves the task itself intact.
how: Find the procedure that needs no decision and print it above the task. For a shortest tour: always go to the nearest place you have not been. For a picture grid: push each run to one end, push it to the other, and the cells filled both ways are certain. For a maze: put your right hand on the wall and never take it off. Say what it gives, because a valid answer to beat and a piece that is certain are different things and only one is final. Then print a second case built so the rule fails — a maze whose goal is ringed by walls touching no edge, where the hand walks sixteen cells and comes home — and ask what the hand did, and why it was enough the first time.

knobs.effect: A mediocre but valid answer, like the nearest-neighbour tour, gives a number to beat and the number improves. A partial but certain answer, like the overlap count, gives cells that will never be taken back. Only the first invites a second attempt.

knobs.knob: whether a failing case is printed too
knobs.effect: One case and the rule is a gift, believed. Two, the second built so it fails, and what comes out is that a procedure can work every time it has been tried and still not be a proof. That is the better half.
Above the task it is a foothold and nobody faces a blank page. Below it, it is a solution and arrives too late to be one. There is no third position that does anything useful.

knobs.knob: whether what the rule scores is printed
knobs.effect: Twenty steps against a shortest twelve, or a tour of 412 mm. Printing the rule's own score turns the task into beating a figure, and nobody is needed afterwards to say whether that happened.

where_the_work_is: In the second case, built so the rule fails. Any handbook prints the rule; printing the maze where the hand walks the outer ring and returns is the part that has to be constructed and checked.
breaks: The rule prints in four lines and fits 800x480; the maze and the ten points do not, and both have to be seen whole. A traced route scans back only if the corridors are drawn well apart. The failing case has to be verified cell by cell before printing — a maze where the hand happens to reach the goal makes the second half of the sheet say nothing, and nobody would notice.
